title: Open windows during cleaner outdoor air windows
evidenceWhy: WHO Housing and Health Guidelines (2021) recommend targeted natural ventilation when outdoor air is cleaner than indoor air to flush accumulated indoor pollutants.
whoBenefits: All household members benefit from reduced indoor CO2 and flushed combustion particulates.
steps: Check the hourly Saans forecast for the daily outdoor PM2.5 trough (typically 12:00-15:00 in winter).
Confirm outdoor PM2.5 is lower than indoor estimate before opening.
Open opposite windows or balcony doors for 15-20 minutes to create cross-ventilation.
Close and latch all windows firmly before outdoor pollution begins its evening surge.

title: Shift outdoor playtime to the lowest-pollution window
evidenceWhy: EPA AirNow and CDC school health guidance recommend scheduling strenuous outdoor activities during daily periods with lowest pollutant concentrations.
whoBenefits: Children and teenagers whose developing lungs and higher respiration rates make them highly vulnerable.
steps: Check the Saans 24-hour timeline to identify the cleanest 2-hour window (usually 13:00 to 15:00).
Reschedule park, playground, or sports activities exclusively to this timeframe.
Limit high-intensity continuous running if AQI is above 150 even during the best window.
Bring children indoors immediately if haze thickens or early evening inversion begins.

title: Switch to indoor active play on severe pollution days
evidenceWhy: CDC wildfire smoke and air quality guidance recommends substituting outdoor exercise with active indoor games to keep children physically active without high pollutant doses.
whoBenefits: Children and toddlers avoiding deep inhalation of fine particulate matter during play.
steps: Designate an indoor play space with closed windows and active air purification.
Introduce low-dust active games such as dance routines, yoga, balloon volleyball, or obstacle courses.
Avoid activities that disturb heavy carpet dust or resuspend floor particles.
Ensure children stay hydrated in well-filtered indoor air.

title: Move workouts indoors during high AQI days
evidenceWhy: EPA Air Quality and Outdoor Activity guidance highlights that heavy exercise increases ventilation rates 4-10x, multiplying pollutant deposition in lower airways.
whoBenefits: Adults, athletes, and anyone engaging in cardiovascular workouts.
steps: Check morning AQI before beginning morning or evening runs/cycles.
Substitute outdoor sessions with indoor treadmill, stationary bike, resistance training, or yoga.
Keep room air purifier running on high during indoor cardio.
If exercising in a gym, verify the facility maintains closed doors and HEPA filtration.

title: Run air purifier on high in bedroom 30 minutes before sleep
evidenceWhy: Multiple randomized crossover trials (Cochrane Review 2021) demonstrate that pre-cleaning bedroom air reduces overnight PM2.5 inhalation by 25-50% and improves sleep cardiovascular markers.
whoBenefits: All family members during 7-9 hours of continuous sleep exposure.
steps: Close bedroom doors and windows firmly 30-45 minutes before bedtime.
Turn the purifier fan speed to Maximum/Turbo to achieve rapid particulate clearance.
Switch fan speed to Low or Sleep mode when going to bed to maintain quiet continuous filtration.
Keep doors closed throughout the night to prevent untreated hallway air from entering.

title: Verify air purifier CADR matches room volume (target 5 ACH)
evidenceWhy: Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM AC-1) and WHO standards specify delivering at least 4-5 Air Changes per Hour (ACH) for meaningful particulate reduction in smoky environments.
whoBenefits: The entire household by preventing false security from undersized air cleaners.
steps: Look up your purifier's clean air delivery rate (CADR in m³/h) on its label or manual.
Calculate your room volume: Area (m²) × Ceiling height (m) = Volume (m³).
Multiply Volume by 5 to calculate minimum required CADR (e.g., 20 m² × 2.7m × 5 = 270 m³/h).
If CADR is below target, either run purifier on highest setting, move it to a smaller closed room, or add a second unit.

title: Replace overdue HEPA filter to restore air cleaning performance
evidenceWhy: EPA Residential Air Cleaners Guide confirms that heavily loaded filters increase fan motor pressure, dramatically decreasing effective CADR and air turnover by 50-80%.
whoBenefits: All room occupants breathing filtered air.
steps: Inspect filter physical discoloration: dark grey/black loading indicates saturated media.
Purchase genuine OEM or certified H13 replacement filter cartridge.
Unplug unit, open compartment, and carefully bag the old filter inside a plastic bag to prevent dust release.
Insert new filter, ensure airtight gasket seating, and reset the unit filter life counter.
safetyNotes: Wear an N95 mask and gloves when removing saturated filters to avoid inhaling accumulated mold spores and heavy particulates.

title: Build a Corsi-Rosenthal DIY box filter for high-volume purification
evidenceWhy: Peer-reviewed aerosol studies (Dal Porto et al. 2022, Environmental Science & Technology) show 4-filter MERV-13 CR boxes achieve 600-800 m³/h CADR at ~20% of commercial HEPA price.
whoBenefits: Budget-conscious households needing high clean air volume for living areas.
steps: Procure one standard 20-inch box fan and four 20x20x2 inch MERV-13 pleated filters.
Arrange the 4 filters into a hollow square base, with arrows pointing inward toward the center.
Duct-tape all corner seams firmly to prevent unfiltered air bypass, and tape a cardboard bottom.
Mount the fan facing upward on top, seal edges thoroughly with duct tape, and run on medium speed.
safetyNotes: Use only modern BIS/UL certified box fans with fused safety plugs.
Never leave DIY electrical fans running unattended overnight or when away from home.
Keep clear of drapery, curtains, and curious children or pets.
Replace MERV-13 filters every 3 to 6 months depending on ambient smoke levels.

title: Keep doors and windows sealed in rooms with active purifiers
evidenceWhy: Indoor aerosol modeling demonstrates that an open door introduces untreated ambient infiltration that degrades effective room clean air delivery by 40-60%.
whoBenefits: Occupants of the designated clean room.
steps: Designate one room (such as the main bedroom) as the primary clean refuge.
Keep bedroom door firmly closed whenever the purifier is operating.
Place a rolled towel or draft stopper across the gap at the bottom of the door.
Minimize repeated entry and exit during high ambient pollution periods.

title: Run kitchen exhaust hood during and 15 minutes after cooking
evidenceWhy: WHO Indoor Air Quality Guidelines (2014) and Lawrence Berkeley National Lab research confirm range hoods capturing cooking plumes cut indoor ultrafine PM and NO2 exposure by 60-85%.
whoBenefits: The family cook and all family members residing in adjacent living spaces.
steps: Switch on the exhaust hood 1 minute before lighting burners or heating oil.
Cook on back burners when possible to maximize capture efficiency into the hood.
Keep kitchen door to living areas closed while cooking.
Keep exhaust fan running on medium for 15 minutes after extinguishing flame to remove residual aerosols.

title: Wet mop hard floors instead of dry sweeping to prevent resuspension
evidenceWhy: EPA Indoor Air Quality assessments show dry sweeping resuspends 80-90% of coarse and fine dust back into human breathing zones, whereas wet microfiber mopping traps particulates.
whoBenefits: Children crawling near floor level and members with hyperreactive airways.
steps: Discontinue traditional dry straw or synthetic broom sweeping during smog season.
Use a damp microfiber flat mop or traditional pocha with clean water.
Rinse the mop frequently in a bucket to avoid spreading trapped sediment.
Allow floors to air-dry naturally without blowing fans directly onto dry dust deposits.

title: Vacuum rugs and upholstery using a sealed HEPA-filtered vacuum
evidenceWhy: EPA Residential Air Cleaners guidance notes non-HEPA vacuums act as aerosol distributors by blowing fine allergens and PM2.5 through standard porous exhaust bags.
whoBenefits: Asthmatics and allergy sufferers sensitive to dust mites and fine settled particulates.
steps: Ensure vacuum cleaner features true sealed HEPA filtration on exhaust output.
Vacuum rugs, mattresses, and cloth sofas 1-2 times weekly with slow overlapping passes.
Empty vacuum canister outdoors or directly inside a closed trash liner to avoid dust clouds.
Wash or replace pre-motor and exhaust HEPA filters per manufacturer schedule.

title: Replace incense sticks and mosquito coils with non-combustion options
evidenceWhy: Aerosol emission research (Jetter et al. 2002; Liu et al. 2003) demonstrates burning 1 mosquito coil releases PM2.5 comparable to 75-100 cigarettes, alongside hazardous polycyclic aromatics.
whoBenefits: Entire family, particularly infants and elderly with coronary or pulmonary conditions.
steps: Switch evening mosquito protection to electric vaporizers, physical window netting, or bed nets.
Replace daily prayer incense with LED diyas, electric camphor diffusers, or fresh flowers.
If burning incense for ceremonial customs, limit to one small natural stick in a well-ventilated space.
Extinguish embers immediately after prayer rituals conclude.

title: Enforce strict 100% smoke-free home policy
evidenceWhy: WHO Secondhand Smoke reports affirm there is zero risk-free exposure level to indoor tobacco smoke; one cigarette elevates room PM2.5 above 300 µg/m³ for hours.
whoBenefits: Non-smoking family members, pregnant women, and developing children.
steps: Establish an unconditional rule: absolutely no smoking inside any room, bathroom, or balcony.
Designate an outdoor location at least 7 meters away from open windows and entry doors.
Wash household draperies, sofa covers, and wipe walls to eliminate persistent third-hand chemical residue.
Support smokers with nicotine replacement therapies or clinical cessation resources.

title: Avoid or disable ionizers and ozone-generating air cleaners
evidenceWhy: EPA Hazardous Ozone Generators Advisory and California Air Resources Board (CARB) warn ozone is a severe pulmonary irritant that scars lung tissue even at low parts-per-billion concentrations.
whoBenefits: Asthmatics, children, and elderly vulnerable to airway inflammation.
steps: Check your air purifier controls for 'Ionizer', 'Anion', 'Plasma', or 'Ozone' toggles.
Switch off ionic or UV-ozone functions permanently; rely exclusively on mechanical HEPA and carbon filtration.
Look for CARB (California Air Resources Board) certification indicating zero ozone emission (<0.050 ppm).
Discard standalone 'air ozonizers' or 'air sanitizers' that market ozone as an odor eliminator.

title: Seal door and window gaps with removable weatherstripping
evidenceWhy: Building science studies (Chen & Zhao 2011) show gap sealing reduces unconditioned aerosol infiltration by 30-50%, dramatically lowering indoor deposition from outdoor smog.
whoBenefits: All household members through reduced baseline indoor pollution penetration.
steps: Identify draft leaks by moving an incense stick or candle along window frames and door perimeter on a breezy day.
Apply self-adhesive EVA foam or silicone weatherstrip tape along matching window sash channels.
Install a silicone sweep or fabric draft stopper under exterior and corridor doors.
Ensure seals compress snugly when windows and doors are latched shut.

title: Transition from biomass cookstoves to LPG or electric induction
evidenceWhy: WHO Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality: Household Fuel Combustion (2014) report biomass stoves cause ~3.8 million premature deaths annually; clean fuel switching cuts cook exposure by 80-95%.
whoBenefits: Primary cooks, infants kept in kitchens, and the entire domestic microenvironment.
steps: Enroll in national clean cooking programs (e.g., PM Ujjwala Yojana) or purchase a dual-burner LPG stove.
Procure a portable 1800W induction cooktop as a convenient soot-free primary or supplemental burner.
Phase out indoor storage and combustion of wood, cow dung patties, and agricultural residues.
Maintain kitchen cross-ventilation while adapting to new clean cooking equipment.
safetyNotes: Check LPG hose connections with soapy water for bubbles every 6 months. Never ignite flames near suspected gas leaks.

title: Wear layered thermal clothing instead of indoor coal or wood fires
evidenceWhy: CDC Carbon Monoxide Prevention warnings emphasize open coal and charcoal braziers (angithis) indoors are the single greatest contributor to lethal winter CO poisoning.
whoBenefits: All family members, especially seniors and small children vulnerable to hypothermia and smoke.
steps: Wear wool or fleece thermal innerwear base layers under regular home clothing.
Wear wool socks, warm slippers, and lightweight beanies to prevent head heat loss indoors.
Use insulated microfiber quilts or hot water bottles inside bedding before sleep.
Completely ban indoor burning of coal, wood, or charcoal briquettes.
safetyNotes: Never light open coal, wood, or charcoal fires inside enclosed rooms. Deadly CO gas is odorless and invisible.

title: Upgrade to an oil-filled or radiant electric heater with auto-shutoff
evidenceWhy: WHO and US CPSC confirm sealed oil-filled electric radiators produce zero combustion emissions, maintaining warmth without depleting oxygen or releasing carbon monoxide.
whoBenefits: Seniors, young children, and individuals with respiratory conditions.
steps: Procure an ISI-certified oil-filled radiator (OFR) or ceramic fan heater with tip-over safety switch.
Plug heater directly into a dedicated 16A grounded wall socket without extension cords.
Set built-in thermostat to comfortable 20-22°C and program timer for bedtime pre-heating.
Maintain a 1-meter clearance around heater away from beds, curtains, and furniture.
safetyNotes: Use only BIS/ISI certified electric heaters with automatic thermal cutoff.
Never drape wet clothes or blankets over heaters to dry.
Do not run electric heating off overloaded multiboards or daisy-chained extension cables.

title: Install an audible digital carbon monoxide (CO) detector
appliesWhen: heating includes 'gas' OR heating includes 'coal_charcoal' OR heating includes 'wood' OR cooking includes 'lpg'
evidenceWhy: CDC Carbon Monoxide safety standards mandate certified CO detectors in all residences using gas, LPG, or combustible heating, reducing poisoning fatality risk by over 50%.
whoBenefits: All household members protected from silent nighttime asphyxiation.
steps: Purchase an EN 50291 or UL 2034 compliant battery-operated digital CO alarm.
Mount alarm on wall at eye/sleeping level (approx 1.5m), 1-3 meters away from kitchen or heater.
Press test button monthly to confirm loud 85dB alarm horn and digital screen operate.
Replace alkaline batteries every 12 months, and replace detector unit every 5-7 years.
safetyNotes: If alarm sounds continuous warning, immediately evacuate all occupants outdoors and call emergency gas utility services.

title: CRITICAL SAFETY: Never seal a room while running combustion heating
appliesWhen: heating includes 'gas' OR heating includes 'coal_charcoal' OR heating includes 'wood'
evidenceWhy: WHO, CDC, and National Disaster Management Guidelines classify sealing rooms containing combustion heating as an immediate life threat due to rapid oxygen depletion and fatal CO accumulation.
whoBenefits: Every resident in the home — this is a non-negotiable life-safety rule.
steps: Always maintain a continuous 2 to 3 cm window gap or door transom opening when any fuel burner is lit.
Never sleep with an active flame, LPG heater, or charcoal angithi inside a closed bedroom.
Extinguish all combustion embers thoroughly and move coals outdoors before going to sleep.
Educate every family member to recognize acute CO poisoning symptoms: dull headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion.
safetyNotes: LIFE THREATENING: Burning coal, wood, or gas in a sealed room creates fatal carbon monoxide poisoning within hours.
If anyone complains of sudden headache, drowsiness, or vomiting while heating is on, move them into fresh outside air immediately and seek emergency medical care.
Never ignore even subtle dizziness around combustion heaters.

title: Wear a certified N95 or FFP2 respirator during outdoor commutes
evidenceWhy: Randomized clinical trials (Langrish et al. 2012, European Heart Journal) demonstrate wearing genuine N95 respirators in urban traffic significantly lowers arterial blood pressure and heart rate variability detriments.
whoBenefits: Two-wheeler riders, cyclists, pedestrians, and open-auto passengers.
steps: Select certified NIOSH N95, EN FFP2, or BIS ISI certified particulate respirators.
Position dual headband straps (one high on crown, one around neck nape) rather than loose earloops.
Mould metallic noseband snugly across bridge of nose using fingers of both hands.
Perform negative pressure seal check: inhale sharply; mask should slightly collapse inward without edge leakage.

title: Perform user seal checks and respect respirator reuse limits
evidenceWhy: NIOSH and CDC respirator research shows facial gaps degrade N95 filtration from ~95% down to ~30%, negating most protection and giving dangerous false security.
whoBenefits: Mask users ensuring their face covering provides rated clinical filtration.
steps: Conduct seal check every single time: cup hands over filter and exhale gently; feel for air leaking onto eyes or chin.
Ensure clean-shaven face along seal border; facial hair dramatically disrupts respirator contact.
Store respirator in a breathable paper bag between commutes; never seal damp in plastic.
Discard respirator after 30-40 hours of active wear, or sooner if stained, deformed, or breathing resistance increases.

title: Apply age-appropriate pediatric respirator guidelines
evidenceWhy: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and WHO caution tight respirators are contraindicated for infants due to suffocation risk; older children require specifically sized pediatric frames.
whoBenefits: Infants, toddlers, and school-age children.
steps: NEVER place any mask, respirator, or cloth covering on infants or toddlers under 2 years of age.
For children aged 3-8, utilize pediatric KN95 or KF94 masks designed specifically for small facial contours.
Prioritize keeping younger children indoors during hazardous AQI over prolonged masking.
Ensure child can easily breathe and speak while masked, and coach them not to chew or touch the inner lining.
safetyNotes: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: Never place masks or respirators on children under 2 years — poses severe suffocation and asphyxiation risk.
If a child shows labored breathing, lethargy, or distress, remove mask immediately and bring indoors into filtered air.

title: Review written asthma and COPD action plans with your physician
evidenceWhy: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA 2022) guidelines establish that written personalized action plans reduce pollution-triggered emergency room admissions by up to 70%.
whoBenefits: Children and adults diagnosed with asthma, chronic bronchitis, or reactive airway syndrome.
steps: Schedule a consultation with your pulmonologist or pediatrician prior to peak winter smog season.
Review peak flow meter thresholds and establish clear green, yellow, and red medication zones.
Verify prescription dosages for maintenance corticosteroid inhalers and fast-acting rescue bronchodilators.
Ensure school nurses or workplace colleagues have access to a backup rescue inhaler and spacer.
safetyNotes: Seek emergency hospital care immediately if rescue inhaler fails to relieve severe breathlessness, chest tightness, or blue discoloration of lips.

title: Shift commute times by 30-45 minutes to avoid peak roadside emissions
evidenceWhy: Health Effects Institute (HEI Special Report 17) demonstrates vehicle exhaust particle counts and black carbon concentrations are 2-4x higher during rush-hour congestion versus shoulder hours.
whoBenefits: Daily commuters reducing transit time and heavy vehicle exhaust exposure.
steps: Coordinate with employer or academic institution for flexible 30-45 minute earlier or later check-in.
Depart prior to 08:00 or after 10:15 in the morning to bypass peak bumper-to-bumper standstill.
Choose secondary residential arterial routes rather than crawling directly behind heavy diesel trucks.
Monitor navigation live traffic overlays to bypass sudden congestion bottlenecks.

title: Switch solo car commute to metro rail or electric transit
evidenceWhy: International Association of Public Transport (UITP 2020) data indicates electric metro transit produces 94% lower per-passenger-km emissions than private cars, with lower in-cabin PM exposure.
whoBenefits: The commuter's health and the broader airshed community through emission abatement.
steps: Map your commute route using public transit navigation apps to identify nearest metro stations.
Purchase a rechargeable smart card or transit pass for seamless turnstile boarding.
Test the metro commute for 2 days mid-week to evaluate transit comfort and exact door-to-door timing.
Adopt metro as primary commute mode on high pollution alert days.

title: Organize a neighborhood carpool for school drop-offs and pickups
evidenceWhy: EPA SmartWay Transportation Partnership notes school gate vehicle clustering creates localized toxic micro-hotspots; carpooling cuts idling vehicles and per-child trips by 50-75%.
whoBenefits: Children exposed to idling tailpipes at school gates and parent drivers saving fuel.
steps: Connect with 3-4 families living in your immediate residential community with children attending same school.
Create a weekly driver roster where each parent handles morning or afternoon runs on rotating days.
Ensure all child passengers wear seatbelts and keep vehicle windows closed with recirculating AC.
Coordinate pickup arrival times via group messaging to avoid unnecessary idling outside school gates.

title: Turn vehicle engine off when waiting at signals or curbside >30 seconds
evidenceWhy: EPA Clean School Bus and Idle-Reduction evaluations demonstrate restarting uses less fuel than 10 seconds of idling, eliminating concentrated toxic CO and benzene emissions around pedestrians.
whoBenefits: Pedestrians, cyclists, children at crossings, and driver's fuel economy.
steps: Turn off the ignition switch at traffic signals showing red countdown timers greater than 30 seconds.
Turn off engine immediately while waiting for passengers curbside or outside retail shops.
Avoid warming up modern vehicle engines for more than 30 seconds in winter; gentle driving warms engines faster.
Encourage auto-rickshaw and cab drivers to cut engines during prolonged snarls.

title: Walk short neighborhood errands only when AQI is moderate or better
evidenceWhy: Health benefit-risk modeling (Tainio et al. 2016, Preventive Medicine) confirms physical exercise benefits outweigh pollution risks when PM2.5 is low, but invert during severe smog episodes.
whoBenefits: Adults seeking active mobility without unnecessary particulate inhalation.
steps: Check current ambient AQI before walking to neighborhood grocery markets or errands.
If AQI is below 100, choose pedestrian walking over two-wheeler or car trips for distances under 1.5 km.
Walk on internal residential colony lanes rather than along heavily trafficked main ring roads.
If AQI unexpectedly rises above 150, postpone non-essential walking or wear an N95 mask.

title: Plan transition from petrol two-wheeler to electric or shared transit
evidenceWhy: ICCT India Emissions Inventory shows 2-wheelers emit ~5x more PM2.5 and CO per km than BS-VI passenger cars due to engine dynamics; electric two-wheelers eliminate tailpipe emissions entirely.
whoBenefits: The commuter (eliminating roadside tailpipe inhalation) and urban community airshed.
steps: Calculate your monthly petrol expenditure and contrast with electric two-wheeler charging costs.
Explore state and national EV subsidy schemes (FAME II / PM E-DRIVE) for upfront capital rebate.
Test ride reliable EV two-wheelers with removable or fast-charging battery packs.
In the interim, use shared metro or bus connections on high pollution alert days.

title: Compost dry leaves and horticultural waste instead of open burning
evidenceWhy: CPCB and WHO environmental reports confirm open burning of biomass and fallen leaves produces massive bursts of carcinogenic dioxins, black carbon, and dense PM2.5 at breathing level.
whoBenefits: Neighborhood residents, ground-floor apartments, and local gardening biodiversity.
steps: Instruct domestic staff and gardeners never to burn dry leaves, twigs, or lawn clippings.
Create a designated wire-mesh compost pit or drum composter in a garden corner or society compound.
Layer brown leaves with green vegetable scraps and moisten periodically with water to accelerate decomposition.
Harvest rich organic humus after 8-12 weeks for potting soil and garden enrichment.

title: Segregate dry and wet household waste at source to prevent landfill burning
evidenceWhy: UNEP Urban Air and Solid Waste reports show unsegregated mixed municipal waste dumping leads to spontaneous landfill fires emitting toxic furans, heavy metals, and persistent smoke.
whoBenefits: Urban community airshed and sanitation workers handling municipal refuse.
steps: Place separate bins in kitchen: Green for organic wet food waste, Blue for dry recyclables.
Rinse recyclable plastic bottles, metal cans, and milk pouches before placing in dry bin.
Dispose of sanitary and hazardous waste in clearly wrapped red bags for separate processing.
Hand segregated bins to municipal collectors or local informal recycling kabadiwalas.

title: Report open waste and leaf burning incidents via citizen grievance apps
evidenceWhy: CPCB enforcement analyses indicate prompt citizen mobile georeporting reduces smoldering burn time by 65%, preventing localized overnight particulate concentration spikes.
whoBenefits: Immediate neighborhood residents downwind of illegal smoldering fires.
steps: Download municipal or state pollution control apps (e.g., Sameer CPCB, Delhi Green, Swachhata).
Safely capture a geotagged photo of the burning garbage, leaf pile, or plastic waste from a distance.
Submit the complaint selecting category 'Open Burning' with precise street landmark details.
Track complaint resolution ticket and escalate to local Resident Welfare Association (RWA) if repeated.
safetyNotes: Do not confront individuals aggressively or attempt to extinguish large industrial/chemical waste fires without protective equipment.

title: Report uncovered construction dust and demolition violations
evidenceWhy: CPCB Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) guidelines mandate green geotextile wind-breaking screens and water misting; reporting enforces dust mitigation protocols.
whoBenefits: Pedestrians, roadside dwellers, and nearby apartment blocks plagued by coarse silica dust.
steps: Identify non-compliant construction sites operating without green mesh screens or uncovered sand/gravel mounds.
Photograph the fugitive dust plumes and missing water sprinkling equipment.
File report via municipal pollution grievance portal or municipal ward helpline.
Engage your neighborhood building society to require local private contractors to follow dust norms.

title: Adopt clean festive celebrations: LED illumination and community gatherings
evidenceWhy: CSIR-NEERI and CPCB Diwali air quality tracking prove traditional fireworks trigger instantaneous PM2.5 spikes exceeding 1500 µg/m³ with toxic barium, strontium, and sulfur oxides.
whoBenefits: Children, pets, seniors, and hospital intensive care patients across urban centers.
steps: Replace chemical pyrotechnics with Warm LED fairy lights, solar lanterns, and decorative flower rangolis.
Organize neighborhood cultural performances, music recitals, or shared community feasts instead of firecracker bouts.
If participating in approved green cracker displays, strictly observe designated 2-hour community windows.
Keep indoor air purifiers running continuously on high throughout festival nights.

title: Organize blanket drives and electric warm-up kiosks for outdoor night guards
evidenceWhy: Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) winter pollution studies show roadside biomass and scrap wood bonfires lit for survival warmth account for significant ground-level evening PM2.5 spikes.
whoBenefits: Outdoor security personnel, sanitation staff, and nearby residential apartments.
steps: Coordinate with building RWA or apartment management to provide electric radiant heaters in guard security booths.
Run a pre-winter society collection drive for heavy blankets, thermal innerwear, gloves, and insulated jackets.
Distribute thermos flasks with hot water and tea to night security and sanitation workers.
Politely request guard staff to retire scrap wood and plastic bonfires in favor of the provided heating amenities.

title: Check on elderly or frail neighbours during hazardous AQI episodes
evidenceWhy: WHO Health Aspects of Air Pollution notes cardiovascular mortality in seniors rises sharply within 24-48 hours of severe particulate episodes; proactive social check-ins save lives.
whoBenefits: Isolated seniors living alone with cardiovascular, hypertensive, or pulmonary conditions.
steps: Call or knock on doors of elderly neighbors when AQI enters Very Unhealthy or Hazardous tiers.
Ensure their windows and balcony doors are latched shut and air purifier (if owned) has power.
Offer to fetch essential groceries, prescription medicines, or clean drinking water to prevent them from venturing out.
Verify emergency contact numbers for family members or attending cardiologists are posted near their phone.

title: Advocate for an AQI-indexed outdoor physical activity policy at your child's school
evidenceWhy: EPA School Flag Program and AAP recommendations advise mandatory cancellation of outdoor sports and morning assemblies when ambient AQI crosses 150-200 to protect child lung alveoli.
whoBenefits: Entire student body, physical education teachers, and staff members.
steps: Draft a collaborative letter to school principal and Parent-Teacher Association citing WHO and CPCB child air guidelines.
Request school shift morning assemblies to classrooms or covered auditoriums when AQI > 150.
Propose replacing vigorous outdoor sports with indoor gym activities whenever AQI exceeds 200.
Suggest installation of a low-cost calibrated AQI monitor in school lobby with colored safety flags.

title: Propose an anti-idling policy inside residential society gates
evidenceWhy: NYC Health Department Anti-Idling evaluations demonstrate campus-level idling bans reduce localized fine particulate concentrations by 15-25% around residential entrances and play lots.
whoBenefits: Residents on lower floors, pedestrians, and children boarding school buses inside gates.
steps: Table an anti-idling resolution at your Resident Welfare Association (RWA) or society committee meeting.
Erect clear 'No Idling Beyond 30 Seconds - Clean Air Zone' reflective signage at entry gates and clubhouse.
Train security gate guards to politely request waiting school cabs, private cars, and delivery vans to cut engines.
Publish an explanatory educational flyer in society communication channels on fuel savings and cleaner lungs.

title: MYTH BUSTED: Indoor plants do NOT clean ambient room particulate pollution
evidenceWhy: Rigorous aerosol physics reviews (Cummings & Waring 2020, Journal of Exposure Science) debunked the 1989 NASA study: plants achieve CADR of ~0.02 m³/h vs HEPA's 250+ m³/h; you would need 600 plants per room.
whoBenefits: Consumers avoiding expensive plant setups in the mistaken belief they replace air purifiers.
steps: Recognize that potted plants cannot draw air through their leaves at rates sufficient to filter fine PM2.5 or VOCs in real homes.
Enjoy houseplants for mental well-being, aesthetics, and humidity moderation rather than air purification.
Do not rely on snake plants, spider plants, or areca palms as substitutes for mechanical HEPA filtration.
Avoid damp soil overwatering in stagnant rooms which can cultivate pathogenic fungal spores.

title: MYTH BUSTED: Inhaling steam does NOT remove PM2.5 particles from lungs
evidenceWhy: AIIMS and pulmonary medical reviews confirm inhaled fine PM2.5 (<2.5 µm) penetrates deep into microscopic alveoli and enters blood circulation; steam condenses in upper airways and cannot 'wash' alveoli.
whoBenefits: Families avoiding false comfort and steam scald injuries.
steps: Understand that steam inhalation reaches only nasal passages and trachea, not microscopic pulmonary alveoli.
Use mild steam only if advised by a clinician to hydrate dry upper mucous membranes or soothe sinusitis.
Never add aggressive chemical oils or camphor into steamers which can induce bronchial spasms.
Focus personal protective efforts on avoiding inhalation through N95 respirators and HEPA air cleaning.
safetyNotes: High risk of hot water scalding and facial burns, especially when administering steam to children. Never use boiling pots on beds.

title: MYTH BUSTED: Jaggery (Gur) and herbal tonics cannot detoxify lungs from PM2.5
evidenceWhy: Lancet Commission on Pollution and Health reviews state dietary intake passes through the gastrointestinal tract and cannot intercept or extract particulate matter lodged in respiratory tissues.
whoBenefits: Individuals avoiding dietary complacency and diabetic patients avoiding unneeded sugar loads.
steps: Understand the physiological separation between the digestive esophagus and respiratory pulmonary tree.
Eat jaggery in moderation as a natural culinary sweetener, but recognize it possesses zero lung-cleaning mechanisms.
Diabetic patients should avoid consuming excessive jaggery doses marketed as 'anti-pollution detox'.
Prioritize exposure reduction: the only proven way to detoxify is breathing cleaner air.

title: MYTH BUSTED: Hanging a wet cloth over windows does NOT filter PM2.5
evidenceWhy: Aerosol filtration experiments (Cherrie et al. 2018) prove coarse woven fabrics allow >85-90% of sub-micron particles to penetrate directly, with airflow taking path of least resistance around fabric edges.
whoBenefits: Households avoiding ineffective DIY barriers and window mold development.
steps: Acknowledge that fine microscopic PM2.5 (0.3 - 2.5 µm) readily slips through the microscopic mesh of woven bedsheets and towels.
Understand that air flows around the edges of hung cloth through large gap clearances.
Avoid damp fabrics against window sills which breed allergenic mold in winter.
Use certified elastomeric weatherstripping to seal window cracks and operate genuine HEPA/MERV-13 filters indoors.
